transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-20
Start time: 09:12 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Emma (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO), Liam (Cloud Architect), Sofia (Security), Noah (SRE)

[00:00] Emma: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro, I'm Emma Clarke, account exec on the Redwood side, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:10] Priya: Good thanks, Emma. Quick note — we wanted this to be focused on the private/VPC side, network readiness and the gating items for compliance.
[00:18] Diego: Great, yep that's what we'll aim for. I'll take the technical details. Before we dive, can you give us a 60-second overview of your infra posture — public cloud provider(s), any multi-region constraints?
[00:30] Liam: Sure. We're primarily on AWS today, account on gov-east and eu-west for data residency. We keep model-inference traffic in a single VPC per region. We use Transit Gateway for most east-west peering between prod VPCs.
[00:45] Noah: We also have an on-prem Kubernetes cluster for low-latency features, but that won't host models, it's mostly for orchestration and telemetry.
[00:52] Diego: Okay that's helpful. Do you have strict egress controls — e.g., only allow specific destinations or require private endpoints for third-party services?
[01:00] Sofia: Yes, outbound is locked down. Anything that leaves the VPC needs an approved private endpoint, or must go through our proxy with mTLS. We also mandate KMS customer-managed keys for any persisted secrets.
[01:12] Emma: Great. At a high level, Redwood Private supports two common patterns: 1) Private endpoints (regional) where we set up interface endpoints in your VPC that talk to our private dataplane, or 2) VPC peering / Transit GW style where we peer and route directly to our dedicated subnets. Both can be combined — we've seen customers use interface endpoints for control plane and peering for high-throughput dataplane.
[01:34] Priya: Can you talk about the IP range footprint? Our networking team is tight on CIDR space.
[01:40] Diego: Absolutely. For a typical Dedicated/Private deployment we ask for a /22 range for the Redwood-managed subnets per region to start, that gives room for scaling. If customers are scarce on space, we can compress to /24s but that sacrifices some HA isolation. Also we can NAT behind your egress if needed to avoid exposing multiple IPs.
[01:58] Liam: /22 per region is quite large for us — we'll probably need to look at shared subnets. Any constraints with overlapping CIDRs?
[02:05] Diego: Overlap is a blocker for peering. If your CIDRs overlap with our intended ranges we can either: a) shift our allocation (if private deployment and you manage the network) or b) use NAT/proxying with a single egress IP for traffic. The cleanest is unique CIDRs.
[02:18] Sofia: Related to that — what's your stance on audit logs and how they're stored? We need logs for all inference requests for compliance audits.
[02:26] Emma: We offer configurable audit logging in Redwood Private. Logs can be pushed to your CloudWatch/S3 with customer-managed KMS, or we can ship to your SIEM via secure connectors. We'll include the ledger options in the security pack.
[02:38] [crosstalk]
[02:40] Priya: Latency question — for inference, we're sensitive to p95 latency under 150ms for short prompts. Which pattern gives best latency: private endpoints or peering?
[02:50] Diego: If you keep the dataplane in the same region and peer directly (Transit GW or VPC peering), you typically see lower p95 compared to hopping through an interface endpoint that goes across AZs. That said, interface endpoints give stronger isolation and easier provisioning in many orgs. Dedicated capacity matters too — a dedicated pool in-region will shave steady-state latency.
[03:10] Noah: We also need to handle restricted regions: we cannot send any customer PII to certain regions. Does Redwood support region pinning?
[03:18] Emma: Yes, you can pin models and serve only in allowed regions with Redwood Private. Our control plane will manage model versioning and routing, but the data plane can be constrained to specified regions. We'll capture your list of disallowed regions in the intake.
[03:32] Liam: On the networking front: our infra prefers Transit Gateway attachments for a single routable plane. Can Redwood integrate with TGW?
[03:40] Diego: Yes, we support Transit Gateway attachments. Two modes: 1) you attach a TGW to a Redwood-managed account — Redwood creates a VPC and attaches to the TGW — or 2) we peer to customer VPCs directly. In both cases we exchange route tables and adhere to your longest-prefix routing. We'll prepare a detailed diagram for the TGW flow.
[03:58] Sofia: Any special ports or FQDNs we need to allow for control plane? Our egress proxy looks up domains.
[04:05] Diego: We'll provide a minimal list. Control plane uses outbound HTTPS to a set of well-known hostnames (we'll include the certs). Dataplane traffic for inference is internal to the peered network, so it's over private IPs if peered, or via interface endpoints if you're using those. TLS is mutual if you opt for mTLS, otherwise we encrypt in transit with TLS.
[04:25] Priya: Regarding KMS — we require customer-managed keys for any persisted model artifacts or logs. Supported?
[04:32] Emma: Yes, Redwood Private integrates with customer KMS/HSM. We'll need an IAM role mapping for access. We'll include step-by-step for granting minimal privileges in the security docs.
[04:42] Liam: A sticky point: procurement. We have to justify cost vs building in-house. Any recommendations on benchmarking?
[04:48] Diego: We can run an apples-to-apples POC: we deploy a small dedicated pool in your region, run your representative prompts, and show token-level cost, p95 latency, and end-to-end throughput. Typical deliverable is a benchmark spreadsheet and a short write-up. For the POC we usually request 2-4 nodes for a week.
[05:06] Priya: Is there a fast path to validate network connectivity without full deployment? Something like a handshake or small test container?
[05:12] Diego: Yes. We can provision a temporary interface endpoint and a small test endpoint that runs a handshake — basic TLS + auth check. That gives you quick confirmation of peering/routing and makes sure egress rules aren't blocking. We call it the network smoke test.
[05:24] Emma: On the compliance side, what's top of mind for you, Sofia?
[05:28] Sofia: SOC 2 coverage obviously, but also separation of customer data, and proof of deletion. We need to know retention windows and whether we can force-delete data. Also SSO integration — we use Okta and want RBAC syncing.
[05:38] Emma: All supported. SOC 2 report and data deletion APIs are in the pack we'll share. Okta SAML/SCIM for provisioning is in the console — we'll show that in the admin walkthrough.
[05:48] [laughs]
[05:50] Noah: One operational question — how do you handle KV cache for chat sessions? We have variable prompt lengths and want to avoid KV blowup across requests.
[05:58] Diego: The runtime supports smart KV eviction policies and prefix caching; you can configure session TTLs and max-kv-size per model. For Private deployments we expose those knobs in the cluster config. We'll include recommended defaults for prompt distributions like yours.
[06:12] Liam: If we go dedicated vs hosted private — what's the difference in network setup?
[06:18] Diego: Hosted Private (Redwood-managed control plane + private dataplane) typically uses interface endpoints for control plane and peering for the dataplane. Dedicated capacity means reserved GPU pools — more predictable performance and often a stable IP space. From networking perspective, dedicated pools still integrate via peering or TGW attachment; main difference is the SLA and committed capacity.
[06:34] Priya: Procurement lead time question — how long to get to an initial pilot assuming we sign?
[06:40] Emma: Once agreements are signed, network provisioning + pilot spin-up is usually 2-3 weeks with your networking team available. If there are complex TGW or cross-account approvals, plan for up to 6 weeks.
[06:51] Sofia: Any example templates for network approvals? We have a change control board that wants specifics.
[06:56] Emma: Yes, we'll include a template network change request (NCR) with the exact CIDRs, route table changes, IAM roles, and a checklist for your change board.
[07:06] Liam: For regions — we still have some EU data residency constraints. If a model endpoint is in eu-west, but control plane touches us in us-west, is that allowed?
[07:16] Diego: Data plane residency is what matters; we can ensure inference traffic and any persisted artifacts stay in eu-west. Control plane metadata (non-PII) can remain in a separate region but we can also run a private control plane per customer if you require stricter separation.
[07:30] Priya: Good. One more on network ops — logging egress to S3 via VPC endpoints, do you have a pattern?
[07:36] Diego: We push logs to your S3 via VPC Gateway endpoints or via Kinesis/Firehose over private links. We'll provide the IAM role and minimal bucket policy required.
[07:46] [inaudible 0:02]
[07:48] Emma: Okay let's map next steps. We'll send the security pack and the NCR template. Diego will produce a TGW vs peering diagram and a short recommendation. Can we schedule the 90-min workshop for next week?
[07:59] Priya: Yes, next Tuesday works for the infra group.
[08:02] Liam: We'll try to get you the CIDRs and egress list by Friday.
[08:06] Emma: Perfect. Any outstanding blockers?
[08:09] Sofia: Procurement budget justification — if you can include a short cost comparison for dedicated vs self-host that's helpful.
[08:15] Diego: We have a one-pager on cost tradeoffs; I'll include that with the diagram.
[08:20] Emma: Awesome, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and the invites.
[08:24] Priya: Thanks, talk soon.

Meeting end.
